evidence: DeformX models DLOs as Cosserat rods; the framework is a direct application of Cosserat rod theory.
Rod engine uses a discrete Cosserat formulation in the Bergou-Audoly DER family (vertices + per-edge SO(3) frames).
Object class targeted by the framework.
Sim-to-real transfer of policies trained in DeformX is the paper's central empirical claim.
Paper proposes the multi-rate Cosserat-rod + Isaac Sim co-simulation pattern; this is the paper's primary architectural contribution.
Rope-swinging hit-target task on UR5e: DeformX vs. Isaac linked-capsule baseline reduces real-world tip-to-goal error from 15.1/25.9/30.4 cm to 6.6/7.3/5.8 cm across three targets, n=10 each.
Paper explicitly proposes and names the Iterative Residual Policy (IRP) framework as its primary contribution.
Paper introduces the Delta Dynamics Network as the specific architectural component that enables IRP.
Real-world results: 1.3-5.5 cm tip-to-goal error across 7 unseen ropes and 2 unseen robot embodiments at iteration 9.
IRP outperforms SysID/SysID_GT in simulation extrapolation and outperforms OptSim oracle on real ropes with un-modeled physics.
Rope is a 1D deformable linear object; cloth manipulation is included as 2D extension.
Core empirical claim space — IRP closes the sim-to-real gap via online adaptation rather than randomization or sysid.
Delta dynamics is structurally a learned Jacobian of trajectories with respect to action perturbations; ILC connection in related work.
Sample-and-evaluate action selection at each iteration is structurally one-step MPC with a learned model.
Visual feedback (rasterized rope-tip trajectory image) drives action refinement across iterations.
Implicit randomization across the (length, density) training grid acts as the simulator-side variation.
MuJoCo's linked-capsule rope (25 capsules) and cloth (13x13 grid) is the simulator's DLO representation.
TossingBot coins the term 'Residual Physics' in Sec. IV-V and demonstrates it on action-space release-velocity residuals.
TossingBot defines the parameterized throwing primitive (release position + velocity, geometric simplifications reducing to scalar release magnitude).
TossingBot uses a closed-form ballistic action prior both as a residual base and as a 128-channel input feature, exemplifying the physics-informed-action-prior pattern.

TossingBot is the source paper for this claim — provides the empirical evidence (84.7% / 82.3% real-world throw success, 87.2% / 83.9% generalization to unseen targets) cited by the claim's evidence field.
Pixel-wise grasp affordance prediction is the perception-to-grasp interface; grasping is the upstream foundation for the joint grasping-throwing learning.
Trains in PyBullet simulation, deploys on real UR5; sim-to-real is structural to the experimental design.
Pick-from-bin + throw of arbitrary geometry sits in the contact-rich manipulation regime; ballistic prior cannot model contact-induced offsets and the residual learns these.
Random object color and placement during training; light DR for visual robustness.
Throw and grasp primitives use a stable, collision-free IK solver to execute the planned end-effector trajectories.

DEFORM's DDER is a methodological component that could plug into DeformX's Cosserat rod engine; both target sim-to-real DLO modeling
both use residual physics — TossingBot at policy level, DEFORM at simulator integrator level
both use residual physics for dynamic DLO problems; IRP at policy/goal level, DEFORM at simulator level
both target DER-based DLO simulation with parameter identification from real data

task-conditioned DLO manipulation; complements DEFORM's dynamics-modeling focus

SoftMimicGen is automated demonstration generation; complements DEFORM's simulator-side calibration

model-based RL self-curriculum; DEFORM provides the kind of accurate model the curriculum could exploit

Free-end-cable / dynamic planar manipulation; complements 3D dynamic DLO modeling
Adapts the bending/twisting energies and quasi-static twist treatment of Bergou et al.'s Discrete Elastic Rods (DER) into MuJoCo via a force-lever conversion to generalized coordinates.
DER discretizes Cosserat rod theory (paper drops stretch and shear, retains bending and twisting); cited as the parent theory of the rod model used here.
Object class targeted by the simulator and the parameter identification pipeline.
Motivation: provide an accurate MuJoCo-native DLO simulation that warm-starts sim-to-real workflows and reduces real-data requirements for downstream learning.
Discussed and rejected as the alternative DLO representation; mass-spring tuning loses physical interpretability.
Discussed as a visually-plausible alternative DLO representation that lacks physical accuracy at large deformations.
Defines the force-lever conversion of DER Cartesian centerline forces to MuJoCo ball-joint torques, plus quasi-static centerline-twist treatment, as the architectural mechanism of the paper.
Three-way validation: localized helical buckling, Michell's instability, and 4-pose real-vs-sim shape comparison on three DLOs, all favoring the adapted DER model over MuJoCo's native cable plugin.
Object class targeted: cables (DLOs) on a planar surface.
Real2Sim2Real is one specific recipe for the broader sim-to-real transfer problem.
Paper explicitly contrasts R2S2R against domain randomization as the alternate sim-to-real strategy.
PyBullet cable model is a chain of capsule rigid bodies with 6-DOF spring constraints — a discrete mass-spring instantiation.
Differential Evolution and Bayesian Optimization are the optimization machinery for Real2Sim parameter tuning.
Paper names and instantiates the three-step Real2Sim2Real pipeline.
Empirically establishes DE-based simulator parameter tuning for cable dynamics, beating Bayesian Optimization in Sim2Sim and serving as the workhorse Real2Sim engine.
Per-cable median tip-error 8/12/14% of cable length on PRC across three cables, 75 trials each. Mixed-data NN policy beats pure-real and pure-sim baselines.
DIDP framework: full-system reduced-order diffusion policy with IL+TO pretraining and physics-informed test-time adaptation; defining contribution of the paper
PITA mechanism: posterior-score augmentation with differentiable physics loss (DDP) plus kinematic boundary condition (KBC), with adaptation restricted to the final projection layer
DIDP wraps the GVS reduced-order rod parameterization (Mathew et al. 2025) for the simulator backbone and to express the differentiable forward kinematics used in PITA
DIDP is built on the goal-conditioned diffusion policy paradigm (Chi et al. 2023); replaces the action-only state with full-system reduced-order state and adds physics-guided test-time adaptation
Object class: 1D rope as a continuum DLO
GVS reduces the Cosserat-rod continuum dynamics into a finite-DoF strain-basis representation
IL+TO learning strategy: imitation learning from 55k expert trajectories provides the diffusion policy's pretraining signal
IL pretraining stage uses behavior cloning on demonstrated full-system trajectories (matched against L_diff)
Reports the headline DIDP results (84.3%@5cm, 20.8%@1cm, 3.6cm mean) on the 3D rope-whipping benchmark
Reports ablations: PITA (DDP+KBC) lifts @5cm from 80.0% to 84.3% over no-TTA baseline; project-only adaptation outperforms full-network finetune at lower cost
Paper frames the dynamic-DLO problem as needing physics-grounded sim-only training with sim-to-real implications, though no real-robot transfer is demonstrated
Pullback tube acceleration is a constrained convex optimization solved at >1 kHz over a short horizon; conceptually a real-time receding-horizon controller (Section IIIC, Tube-CVX program).
Three-layer stack mixes model-free RL (PPO nominal + residual) with a model-based optimizer (pullback tube QP).
Standard sim-to-real techniques applied to both nominal and residual training stages, including domain randomization, observation noise, and symmetry augmentation (Section III-D).
Actuator networks, observation noise, and symmetry augmentation listed as standard sim-to-real techniques applied; residual policy explicitly flagged as suffering a sim-to-real gap.

Gripper-object detachment uncertainty (50-100 ms detach window from screw drive fingers + variable normal-force vanishing time) is a contact-uncertainty problem central to the paper's release-time model.
Robotiq 2f140 prehensile gripper used; release-time uncertainty is bounded by the 50 ms gripper dwell time and material deformation.
The 400 Hz residual policy on top of a frozen 100 Hz nominal is named and contributed in this paper (Section III-B High-frequency Residual Policy and contribution bullet 2 in introduction).
Pullback Tube Acceleration is named in Section III-C as the closed-loop variant of Liu and Billard's open-loop tube acceleration; the convex Tube-CVX program is the paper's contribution.

Paper formulates whole-body prehensile throwing as time-dependent EE state tracking on the goal manifold of object flight; first reported instance of prehensile whole-body throwing with quantified hardware accuracy (conclusion).

40 timed throws across 4 ground-target locations (4 m and 6 m forward, ±0.5 m lateral); mean landing error 0.276 m at 6 m, 0.429 m at 4 m for full stack vs 0.685 m / 0.710 m for nominal-only baseline; 49.5% accuracy improvement; 1500-condition simulation grid shows monotonic landing error reduction with pullback control rate; human comparison: robot 56.8% vs humans 15.2% (Section IV).

Pinocchio inverse-dynamics analysis of 5 throws at 10 m/s horizontal velocity: legged base contributes 51.7 N*m*s of angular momentum and 46.3 J of work prior to release; 53.4% higher angular impulse than tabletop manipulator running same joint trajectory; base remains stationary at low velocities and tilts as commanded velocity grows (Section IV-C, Fig. base_motion).
